title: Lena and the Uniform
premise: In 1899, in a port city on the brink of uprising, Beatrix Oyelaran works quietly cutting type in her father's print shop, content to be invisible. When a sealed letter hidden in a delivery of lead names her family as keepers of evidence against the colonial governor, she cannot stay out of it: the courier who brings the letter, Elias, is the son of the officer assigned to burn the shop down. Falling for him means betraying her father's cause; protecting her father means deceiving the only man who has ever seen her. At the century's turn, Beatrix smuggles the letter past three checkpoints sewn into her late mother's uniform coat, and must choose between exposing the truth and saving Elias from his own loyalty — ending with the letter published, the father arrested but alive, and Elias choosing her over the uniform.
about_author: Paloma Villalobos is a former typesetter who spent a decade restoring letterpress equipment in coastal archives before turning to fiction. She writes historical novels about ordinary hands that move history, and lives near a defunct print works she refuses to call a museum.

chapters.title: The Weight of Lead
chapters.summary: Beatrix's POV. In the print shop's final week of the year, Beatrix cuts type by lamplight while revolution murmurs outside; a delivery of lead arrives with a sealed letter stitched inside a soldier's discarded uniform coat, addressed to her dead mother. The emotional beat is quiet dread — the discovery that invisibility was always an illusion.

chapters.title: Three Checkpoints
chapters.summary: Alternating POV between Beatrix and Elias. The letter must reach a printer across the river before New Year's Eve; Elias, wearing his officer father's uniform, offers to walk her through the checkpoints he knows by heart. Each gate they pass tightens their bond and the danger, as soldiers begin hunting a girl and a deserter. The beat is breathless intimacy built on mutual deception.

chapters.title: What the Coat Remembers
chapters.summary: Elias's POV. At the second checkpoint, Elias's father recognizes the uniform's missing buttons and gives his son until midnight to surrender the girl and the letter. Torn between inherited duty and the truth he has read in the letter — that his own regiment burned a village to protect the governor — Elias hides Beatrix in the barracks. The beat is betrayal curdling into conviction.

chapters.title: Midnight Type
chapters.summary: Beatrix's POV. At the third checkpoint, Beatrix walks through alone wearing her mother's uniform coat, the letter against her heart, while Elias stands at attention and lets her pass — then tears off his insignia and follows. The letter is set and printed as church bells ring in 1900; her father is taken, but the truth runs free in ten thousand copies. The beat is grief braided with hard-won hope.
